cases.purpose: Different scripts per side by design: the reference side is the independent oracle (Tcl Expect 5.45 from the Debian 'expect' package driving the same trusted child), the candidate side is the bash-os expect builtin; both write the same semantic record file 'out', which the tree comparison checks byte for byte. Dialog: a ready 'beta alpha id=42' line tested with patterns alpha, beta (first listed wins) and zzz, id=[0-9]+ (capture); 'split-ok' arriving as 'spl' then 'it-ok' 300 ms later; timeout 0 consuming ready 'late-token' and timing out at once on an absent pattern. Correction after batch37: every expect(1) call passes pattern/action pairs as separate arguments; the first version used one-line single braced lists (and '-timeout N {list}'), which expect(1) treats as a single glob pattern, so no action ran.
cases.oracle: Independent oracle: Tcl Expect (expect(1)): patterns of one expect command are tested in the order listed; -re captures in expect_out(0,string); timeout bounds the expect command; timeout 0 examines available input without waiting; eof is distinct from timeout; close + wait reports the child's exit status or CHILDKILLED signal. The candidate's documented mapping (expect.c expect_doc): 0 match, 1 timeout, 2 EOF; eof 0/1; close returns status or 128+N. Tcl's consuming buffer differs from the candidate's retained buffer, so every dialog uses patterns whose outcome is the same under both buffer policies.
cases.comparison: parity of semantic records vs Tcl Expect (independent oracle): which pattern, capture, spanning match, zero-timeout statuses and promptness, EOF and close status

Dialog: continuous 'x' output every 50 ms against a 3 s timeout; a silent live child (eof and expect time out after 1 s); EOF arriving well before a 10 s deadline for expect and, on a second child, for eof. Correction after batch37: every expect(1) call passes pattern/action pairs as separate arguments; the first version used one-line single braced lists (and '-timeout N {list}'), which expect(1) treats as a single glob pattern, so no action ran. Correction after batch46: Expect 5.45.4 keeps the expect deadline in whole seconds (expect.c: end_time = Tcl_GetTime().sec + timeout; remtime recomputed from .sec after every read, timeout once remtime < 0), so under continuous output a -timeout T wait ends at a second boundary in (T-1, T] s; the continuous-output segment now uses T = 3 on both sides and the predicate 1.9 s <= elapsed < 4.0 s, which still rejects a timer reset by output (no timeout at all) and an early return. The candidate's finer 0.9-2.0 s bound for -t 1 remains asserted by the executed contract case migration-expect-deadline-and-eof.

The candidate's documented mapping (expect.c expect_doc): 0 match, 1 timeout, 2 EOF; eof 0/1; close returns status or 128+N. Tcl's consuming buffer differs from the candidate's retained buffer, so every dialog uses patterns whose outcome is the same under both buffer policies. Expect's timeout clock has one-second resolution (expect.c 5.45.4, Exp_ExpectObjCmd timeout loop): with continuous non-matching output the wait ends within (T-1, T] s, with a silent child after T s.

files.rt.py:
import os, signal, sys, time
def w(s): os.write(1, s.encode())
mode = sys.argv[1]
if mode == 'dialog':
    leader = os.getsid(0) == os.getpid() and os.isatty(0) and os.tcgetpgrp(0) == os.getpgrp()
    try:
        os.close(os.open('/dev/tty', os.O_RDWR)); ctty = 'yes'
    except OSError:
        ctty = 'no'
    w('leader=%s ctty=%s pid=%d\n' % ('yes' if leader else 'no', ctty, os.getpid()))
    w('name? ')
    w('got=%r\n' % os.read(0, 100).decode())
    w('cmd? ')
    w('got2=%r\n' % os.read(0, 100).decode())
    sys.exit(7)
if mode == 'killself':
    w('ready\n')
    os.kill(os.getpid(), signal.SIGTERM)
    time.sleep(5)
if mode == 'linger':
    w('ready\n')
    time.sleep(30)
    sys.exit(3)
